eval.Base rate: what if violations were rare:
This dataset is 57.1% flag; a real expense stream has a few percent. 0 false flag(s) among 12 non-flag receipts is compatible with a false-alarm rate of up to 26.5%; with sensitivity and specificity both at their lower bounds, the share of A's flags that are real (PPV) at 1.0%, 3.0%, 10.0% prevalence falls to 2.9%, 8.5%, 25.0%: the false-positive numbers above say little about what reviewers would see. The keyword baseline's measured specificity (83.3%) already gives a point PPV of 12.2% at 3.0%. Before production I would measure per-rule precision on a random, not enriched, sample of real receipts checked by auditors, the review-queue workload (flag + review per 1,000 receipts), drift in the classifier's confidence bands and category mix over time, and cost per receipt (the last held-out run cost $0.00053 per receipt).

PPV = sens·p / (sens·p + (1−spec)(1−p)). Sensitivity and specificity are the measured ones below; the PPV range plugs in both lower CP bounds and both upper CP bounds (PPV rises in both). A specificity of 100% means no false alarm was *observed* among few negatives, not that there are none; the lower bound is what to plan with.

eval.How to read this:
- **Tiny n, one run.** 28 receipts, 9 pass / 16 flag / 3 review. An interval spanning 30 points is the honest size of what we know. Per-class figures on the 3 review receipts are anecdotes, not rates. A bootstrap of a perfect score is degenerate (`boot[100%, 100%]`: every resample is perfect); for those, read the Clopper-Pearson bound.
- **Only the classifier is measured blind.** The rule engine was written with this dataset (and its answers) in view, so B ORACLE is a consistency check of the engine against the answers, not an estimate of how it generalises. A LLM is the only number where the measured component never saw the answers (prompt = taxonomy text only), and even there the taxonomy's own examples sit in the prompt.
- **The keyword baseline (C) was frozen before scoring** (sha256 of its table and compiled patterns pinned in tests). It feeds the same engine, so A vs C isolates the classifier; differences are measured on the same 28 receipts and are paired. C maps descriptions to all 21 categories (restricted words tried first), because the engine and macro F1 need a category, not just a yes/no.
- **The dataset is enriched:** 16/28 = 57.1% flag. The base-rate tables below are a what-if, not a measurement.
- The held-out stress test (last section) is a separate set written by a single annotator; its expected labels are one person's judgement.

eval.Two failure cases:
A LLM gets none of the 28 scored receipts wrong, so case 1 is the one receipt the engine gets wrong when fed perfect categories, and case 2 comes from the held-out set, where the classifier does make errors. The keyword baseline's errors (above) belong to a system this project replaces.

**1. RCP-022 under B ORACLE. Stage: classification, as the input to the rule logic.** Correct flag with GIFT-04; B gives pass with nothing fired; A gives flag with GIFT-04. Every category is right in B, yet the rule cannot fire: who received the items is stated only in the line text, and gold line labels carry the category alone. A gets it right only because the classifier also returns the stated recipient (RCP-022-L1: government_official, RCP-022-L2: government_official). So the category is not the whole input the engine needs, and a perfect category score would not have caught this. On the held-out set that recipient output is right in 5/5 stated cases and invented on 1/139 lines with none stated. Change: treat the recipient as a scored classifier output with its own test set, and take it from a structured field at submission when one exists, so an anti-corruption exception never rests on one free-text reading.

**2. Held-out lines the classifier gets wrong (prompt v3; single-annotator labels, not dataset-scored receipts). Stage: classification.** 7 of 144 lines differ from the annotator's category: HO-008-L4 'Gel hydroalcoolique 100ml' -> health_otc, annotator personal_care; HO-011-L5 'Shoe shine' -> personal_care, annotator laundry_service; HO-020-L2 'Set de regalo' -> other, annotator gift; HO-021-L2 'Gravur' -> other, annotator service_fee; HO-024-L1 'Compute credits top-up (prepaid)' -> other, annotator software_subscription; HO-026-L4 'ウコンの力' -> health_otc, annotator food_beverage; HO-039-L1 'Coffret dégustation' -> alcohol, annotator gift. 7 of them are one of the annotator's listed alternatives, so the lenient score counts them right. They were rated low 3, medium 4, and only `low` raises EXC-03, so the uncertainty route catches 3 of 7. 3 cross the restricted boundary (HO-008-L4, HO-011-L5, HO-020-L2). Fed to the engine with the annotator's recipients held fixed, the predicted categories change the rule outcome on 5 receipt(s), compared with the annotator's categories: HO-008: PERS-01 cites HO-008-L1, HO-008-L2 instead of HO-008-L1, HO-008-L2, HO-008-L4; HO-011: review -> flag, LAUNDRY-01 no longer fires, PERS-01 fires on HO-011-L5; HO-020: DOC-03 fires; HO-024: TECH-04 cites HO-024-L2 instead of HO-024-L1, HO-024-L2; HO-039: ALC-03 fires on HO-039-L1, DOC-03 fires, GIFT-01 cites HO-039-L2 instead of HO-039-L1, HO-039-L2. Separately, a recipient was attached to 1 line(s) that state none (HO-004-L1 'Wine': client J. Okafor); with the annotator's categories held fixed this gives: no rule outcome changes. Had the copied recipient been a government official, GIFT-04 (critical) would cite HO-004-L1 (alcohol). Change proposed, not applied: ask the classifier for a runner-up category per line and raise EXC-03 when the top and runner-up categories disagree on `restricted`, not only when it says `low`; measure, on a fresh held-out set, how many restricted-boundary errors that catches against how many correct lines it sends to review. Score the recipient per line as its own classifier output, with lines next to a named recipient on purpose, so a recipient copied to a sibling line counts as an error.
eval.What a score of 1.000 does and does not: A's macro F1 of 1.000 and 28/28 dispositions mean that, in this one run, the classifier gave the engine the category it needed on all 65 scored lines and the engine turned them into the right answer. They do not mean the system is always right. The engine was written with these receipts and their answers in view, so its share of the score is consistency with the answers, not generalisation; the classifier is the only blind component, and its prompt holds the taxonomy's own examples. It is one run of a sampled model, on n = 28 receipts: the 95% lower bounds are 87.7% for dispositions and 94.5% for line categories. The held-out set is the better estimate of the classifier: 137/144 = 95.1% [90.2%, 98.0%] exact there.
eval.What each score says about whether the e:
- **Macro F1 on categories** (A 1.000, C 0.776). The category is the input every category-keyed rule reads (alcohol, technology, personal, gift, health ...), so this is the most direct measure of whether the engine is fed correctly: A gave the engine a wrong category on 0 of 65 lines. Every category counts equally, and 13 of the 19 categories have two lines or fewer, so one wrong line in a rare category moves the score by up to 1/19; it measures this data, not the taxonomy.
- **F1 on restricted = true** (A 1.000, C 0.821). Only errors that cross the restricted boundary count, and those decide whether a restricted-item rule can fire at all. C called 5 restricted line(s) unrestricted (the rule then cannot fire: a missed violation) and 2 unrestricted line(s) restricted (material for a false alarm). A category error inside one side of the boundary (gift vs jewelry) leaves this score unchanged and can still change which rule fires.
- **Disposition accuracy** (A 28/28, B 27/28, C 21/28). End to end: inputs and engine together. B feeds perfect categories, so every B error is an input the engine needs beyond the category, or an engine error: B gets RCP-022 wrong (failure case 1). A and C share the engine, so the A-C gap (7 receipts A right and C wrong, 0 the other way) is all classifier.
- **False positives** (A 0/9, C 1/9 of 9 pass). A false alarm on a clean receipt needs a wrong input that triggers a rule. C's: RCP-004 ('Beer battered cod & chips' -> alcohol, correct food_beverage, 'Arnold Palmer' -> other, correct food_beverage, 'Mojito sin alcohol' -> other, correct food_beverage, 'Rum cake slice' -> alcohol, correct food_beverage). A's 0/9 has an upper bound of 33.6%: with 9 clean receipts this data cannot rule out roughly one false alarm in 3 clean receipts.
- **Missed violations** (A 0/16, C 4/16 of 16 flag). A miss is an input the engine needed and did not get. C's: RCP-010 ('Draft IPA 16oz' -> other, correct alcohol); RCP-022 (every category right); RCP-024 ('Marlboro Gold pack' -> other, correct tobacco); RCP-025 ('Schweinebraten mit Knoedel' -> other, correct food_beverage, 'Weisswein 0,2l' -> other, correct alcohol, 'Mineralwasser 0,5l' -> other, correct food_beverage). A's upper bound is 20.6%.
- **Baseline gap.** C is wrong on 16 of 65 lines; on 13 of them no keyword matched (`other`), on 3 a keyword matched something the item is not, and 6 are non-English. Where the keyword baseline does better than the LLM (point estimates): nowhere on these measures. It is free, deterministic and needs no network, which the LLM is not.

ALC-01.text: ALC-01 — Alcohol requires a documented entertainment context. Alcohol is reimbursable only on a receipt declared as Client Entertainment that records an attendee count of two or more. Alcohol on any other receipt — an individual or team meal, or any receipt without an attendee count — is a high exception.
ALC-01.title: Alcohol requires a documented entertainment context

ALC-02.text: ALC-02 — Alcohol per-attendee cap. Where alcohol is permitted under ALC-01, it is capped at $30 per attendee: the USD total of the alcohol lines, divided by the attendee count. Spend above that cap is a medium exception.
ALC-02.title: Alcohol per-attendee cap

ALC-03.text: ALC-03 — Retail alcohol. Alcohol purchased from a package store, liquor store, or any other merchant that is not a restaurant, bar or hotel is never reimbursable, regardless of business context. This is a high exception. See also MCC-01 in merchant-category-risk.md.
ALC-03.title: Retail alcohol

DOC-01.text: DOC-01 — Itemization threshold. Any receipt with a total above $75 (in USD) must be itemized. A non-itemized receipt above that threshold is a medium exception, because the contents cannot be audited.
DOC-01.title: Itemization threshold

DOC-02.text: DOC-02 — Legibility. A receipt must show the merchant name, the transaction date, and the total. A receipt missing any of these is a medium exception.
DOC-02.title: Legibility

DOC-03.text: DOC-03 — Expense type must match the contents. A receipt is misclassified when none of its line items belongs to a category that its declared expense type covers. Service fees, gratuities and items in the other category are ignored for this test; if no items remain, DOC-03 does not apply. A misclassification is a medium exception, reported in addition to any exception raised by the items themselves, not instead of it.
DOC-03.title: Expense type must match the contents

DOC-04.text: DOC-04 — Foreign currency. Receipts in a currency other than USD must record the transaction currency and the conversion rate used; a receipt missing either is a medium exception. All policy thresholds are evaluated on the USD converted amount.
DOC-04.title: Foreign currency

ENT-01.text: ENT-01 — Entertainment venues. Golf, sporting events, theatre, concerts, and similar venue spend requires prior VP approval, recorded as an approval reference (see EXC-02). Without one this is a medium exception.
ENT-01.title: Entertainment venues

ENT-02.text: ENT-02 — Gambling. Gambling spend of any kind is prohibited and is a high exception.
ENT-02.title: Gambling

EXC-01.text: EXC-01 — Receipt disposition. A receipt's disposition is determined by the most severe exception raised against it:
EXC-01.title: Receipt disposition

EXC-02.text: EXC-02 — Approval references. Every approval or exception reference — a pre-approval, a VP or manager approval, or a baggage-delay reference — is recorded in one field on the expense (pre_approval_ref in the data). Where a rule requires such a reference, a recorded one satisfies that rule and no exception is raised — provided it is the kind the rule asks for: a pre-approval for TECH-02, a VP approval for ENT-01, a manager approval for TECH-04, a baggage-delay reference for the PERS-01 and PERS-02 carve-outs. A reference does not waive any other rule.
EXC-02.title: Approval references

EXC-03.text: EXC-03 — Uncertainty. Where the category of an item cannot be determined with sufficient confidence, raise a review signal with rule ID EXC-03 rather than an exception, and leave that item out of every other rule's calculation for the receipt. A non-itemized charge is not an uncertain category: it is other by definition, and raises no EXC-03 signal. An unnecessary exception costs a reviewer's time and erodes trust in the system; a missed review costs far less than a false accusation against an employee.
EXC-03.title: Uncertainty

EXC-04.text: EXC-04 — Evidence. Every exception must cite the rule identifier, the policy document it comes from, and the line items it concerns. An exception that cannot name its evidence must not be raised.
EXC-04.title: Evidence

GIFT-01.text: GIFT-01 — Client gift cap. Gifts to clients and prospects are capped at $50 per recipient per occasion. An occasion is one receipt; lines on it that name the same recipient are added together for the cap, and the $10 test applies to each line. Spend above the cap is a medium exception. Any gift of $10 or more must also name its recipient, in the line description or elsewhere on the expense; an unnamed gift at that value is a medium exception. Cards and small tokens under $10 need no named recipient. Gift cards and other cash equivalents fall under GIFT-02 alone and are not also tested here. Unnamed gifts are each tested on their own, and when both parts of GIFT-01 apply, one exception cites every line involved.
GIFT-01.title: Client gift cap

GIFT-02.text: GIFT-02 — Gift cards and cash equivalents. Gift cards, prepaid cards, vouchers, and any other cash equivalent are never reimbursable, at any amount and for any recipient. This is a high exception.
GIFT-02.title: Gift cards and cash equivalents

GIFT-03.text: GIFT-03 — Employee gifts and awards. Recognition gifts for employees must be processed through HR and are not reimbursable on an expense report. This is a medium exception.
GIFT-03.title: Employee gifts and awards

GIFT-04.text: GIFT-04 — Government officials. Gifts, meals, or anything of value provided to a government official, public employee, or state-owned enterprise employee are prohibited under our anti-corruption policy, at any amount. The exception cites every line provided to the official — including a meal line that also covers the employee's own meal, but not a gratuity (EXC-04) — and replaces GIFT-01 for those lines. Other rules, such as the meal cap, still apply to the receipt. This is a critical exception and is routed to Compliance immediately, never to the standard audit queue.
GIFT-04.title: Government officials

HEALTH-01.text: HEALTH-01 — Over-the-counter medication. OTC medication is reimbursable only on a receipt linked to a trip, up to $25 in total across all of that trip's receipts. Above $25, or on a receipt with no trip record, it is a low exception, raised on each such receipt and citing its medication lines. Prescription medication is never reimbursable on an expense report and is a medium exception.
HEALTH-01.title: Over-the-counter medication

HOUSE-01.text: HOUSE-01 — Household goods. Cleaning supplies, laundry products, household paper goods (paper towels, toilet paper, tissues), kitchenware and drinkware, bedding, furniture, small appliances, and home décor are not reimbursable, whether bought for home or for an office — office stock of this kind is bought centrally. This is a medium exception.
HOUSE-01.title: Household goods

LAUNDRY-01.text: LAUNDRY-01 — Laundry and dry cleaning. Reimbursable only on trips of four or more nights, using the trip length on the receipt. On shorter trips, or on a receipt with no trip record, it is a low exception.
LAUNDRY-01.title: Laundry and dry cleaning

MCC-01.text: MCC-01 — High-risk merchant category. A transaction at a high-risk MCC raises a high exception on its own, whatever the line items say. These categories are not consistent with any routine business purpose.
MCC-01.title: High-risk merchant category

MCC-02.text: MCC-02 — Medium-risk merchant category. A medium-risk MCC raises a review signal only. It is not an exception by itself and must never be reported as one; it exists to prioritise sampling and to add context to an exception raised by another rule. It is always reported as its own review signal, even when another rule raises an exception on the same receipt.
MCC-02.title: Medium-risk merchant category

MCC-03.text: MCC-03 — Bars and taverns. A bar (MCC 5813) serves alcohol on the premises, so ALC-01 and ALC-02 apply to it exactly as they do to a restaurant, and it is never treated as retail under ALC-03.
MCC-03.title: Bars and taverns

MEAL-01.text: MEAL-01 — Daily meal cap. Meal spend is capped at $75 per person per day for domestic travel and $100 per person per day for international travel. Spend above the cap is a medium exception. For this rule:
MEAL-01.title: Daily meal cap

MEAL-02.text: MEAL-02 — Attendee documentation. Any meal receipt (as defined in MEAL-01) whose receipt total is above $150 in USD must record the number of attendees. A missing attendee count is a low exception.
MEAL-02.title: Attendee documentation

PERS-01.text: PERS-01 — Personal care and grooming. Toiletries, cosmetics, razors, haircuts, salon services, spa treatments, and massage are not reimbursable. This is a medium exception.
PERS-01.title: Personal care and grooming

PERS-02.text: PERS-02 — Clothing and footwear. Clothing, footwear, and fashion accessories such as belts, ties and bags are not reimbursable; a medium exception. The same $150 baggage-delay exception applies: one $150 allowance per delay, shared between toiletries and clothing. Above it, the exception cites every line involved.
PERS-02.title: Clothing and footwear

PERS-03.text: PERS-03 — Tobacco and vaping. Cigarettes, cigars, loose tobacco, vaping devices and e-liquids are not reimbursable. This is a high exception.
PERS-03.title: Tobacco and vaping

REG-01.text: REG-01 — Alcohol. Alcohol is never reimbursable for APAC-entity employees, including within client entertainment. This overrides ALC-01 and ALC-02: where those rules would have permitted alcohol with an attendee count, REG-01 still makes it a high exception. For APAC employees REG-01 replaces ALC-01, ALC-02 and ALC-03: report REG-01 instead of those three. Rules about the merchant, such as MCC-01, still apply.
REG-01.title: Alcohol

REG-02.text: REG-02 — Meal cap. The APAC daily meal cap is $60 per person, replacing both MEAL-01 figures for APAC employees. Meal spend, per person and per day are defined as in MEAL-01. A breach is a medium exception, reported as REG-02, not MEAL-01.
REG-02.title: Meal cap

REG-03.text: REG-03 — Meal cap. The EMEA daily meal cap is EUR 70 per person, replacing both MEAL-01 figures for EMEA employees. Convert EUR 70 to USD at the euro rate on the transaction date — for a euro receipt, that is the receipt's own rate — before comparing. Meal spend, per person and per day are defined as in MEAL-01. A breach is a medium exception, reported as REG-03, not MEAL-01.
REG-03.title: Meal cap

REG-04.text: REG-04 — VAT documentation. Receipts above EUR 50 — converted at the euro rate on the transaction date for a receipt in another currency — must be valid VAT receipts showing the merchant VAT number. A missing VAT number is a low exception. Where the expense record does not capture a VAT number, treat it as missing.
REG-04.title: VAT documentation

REG-05.text: REG-05 — Conversion rate. Currency conversion uses the rate on the transaction date, which must be recorded on the expense record. REG-05 says which rate to use and raises nothing on its own; a missing rate is reported under DOC-04.
REG-05.title: Conversion rate

TECH-01.text: TECH-01 — Personal electronics are not reimbursable. This includes, and is not limited to: headphones and earbuds, smart watches and fitness trackers, tablets and e-readers, games consoles, cameras and drones, televisions, portable speakers, and item trackers. Accessories made for such a device — cases, chargers, screen protectors — count as personal electronics too. Purchase of any of these on an expense report is a high exception, regardless of stated business purpose.
TECH-01.title: Personal electronics are not reimbursable

TECH-02.text: TECH-02 — Peripherals under $200. Computer accessories and peripherals — cables, adapters, docking stations, mice, keyboards, monitors, laptop stands, webcams — are reimbursable up to $200 per item, judged on the item's unit price in USD. Any accessory or peripheral above $200 requires a pre-approval reference (see EXC-02); without one it is a medium exception.
TECH-02.title: Peripherals under $200

TECH-03.text: TECH-03 — Mobile handsets. Mobile phone hardware is procured centrally by IT and is never reimbursable on an expense report. This is a high exception.
TECH-03.title: Mobile handsets

TECH-04.text: TECH-04 — Software subscriptions. Any software or SaaS subscription on an expense report requires a manager approval reference (see EXC-02). Without one this is a low exception.
TECH-04.title: Software subscriptions

TIME-01.text: TIME-01 — Overnight transactions. A transaction timed from 00:00 up to, but not including, 05:00 raises a review signal. Transaction times are recorded in local time at the merchant.
TIME-01.title: Overnight transactions

TIME-02.text: TIME-02 — No associated trip. An individual travel expense — declared as Meals - Individual, Lodging, or Travel - Other — with no associated trip record raises a review signal. Team meals and client entertainment often happen without travel and are not covered.
TIME-02.title: No associated trip

TIME-03.text: TIME-03 — Split transactions. Two or more receipts by the same employee, at the same merchant (by merchant name), on the same calendar date, are treated as a deliberate split when each one is at or below one of these thresholds but together they are above it: the $75 itemization threshold, when every receipt in the group is non-itemized (DOC-01); the employee's meal cap, compared per person (MEAL-01, REG-02, REG-03); or the $50 gift cap for one recipient (GIFT-01). This is an exception, at high severity, and applies to every receipt in the group. It replaces the threshold rule being split around: report the split, not a separate breach of that threshold.
TIME-03.title: Split transactions

TIME-04.text: TIME-04 — Weekend spend on a weekday trip. A transaction dated on a weekend that falls outside the trip's recorded start and end dates raises a review signal. It applies only when the trip record includes those dates; where there is no trip record at all, TIME-02 covers it.
TIME-04.title: Weekend spend on a weekday trip
